output.brief: The evidence points mainly at the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Applications, admits and admitted GPA all rose, so the applicant pool was not the problem. Yield fell in the two tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's went from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Yield held steady in the Presidential tier (awards unchanged) and among students with no merit award. Early-action yield fell almost as much as regular-decision yield (45.2% to 37.8% versus 39.0% to 31.5%). Early-action decisions ran on the prior-year timetable and were not delayed, so slow regular-decision answers cannot explain the drop. The portal and staffing delays were real and hurt some students, but they do not explain the shortfall. I am fairly confident (about 80%). The tier data does not split early action from regular decision, and the missing-transcript claim is untested. Next steps: do not replace the director on this basis. Take the scholarship schedule back to the finance committee, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Separately, set a turnaround target for regular decision and have the vendor investigate the transcript problem.
